opus-5.5.text:
I think they're well-intentioned, and I signed some of those letters myself, but I'm not optimistic about what they can actually achieve. Look at the structure of the problem. You have enormous economic incentives, a handful of very well-funded labs, and geopolitical competition between nations, and everyone believes that if they slow down, someone else will get there first. That's a classic race dynamic, and races are very hard to stop with letters and voluntary commitments.

Regulation, as it's usually proposed, also tends to focus on the wrong things. We regulate bias, privacy, misinformation, copyright. Those are real issues, but they're the problems of today's narrow tools. My concern is with systems that are more capable than us across every domain. You can't regulate your way out of the fact that we don't know how to control something smarter than us. Saying "you must make it safe" is meaningless if nobody knows how to do that. It's like passing a law requiring perpetual motion machines to be energy efficient.

Then there's enforcement. Compute is getting cheaper, algorithms are getting more efficient, and much of this research is published openly. Even if you cap the biggest training runs today, in a few years the same capability may fit on far less hardware. So a pause buys time, and time is valuable, but it doesn't solve the underlying problem unless we use that time to figure out whether control is even possible. My research suggests it may not be, at least not with the guarantees we'd want.

So what would I like to see? Honestly, I'd like the people building these systems to look at their own self-interest. These aren't evil people. Many of them say there's a meaningful chance this goes catastrophically wrong, including for them and their families. If you believe that, the rational thing isn't to build it faster. You can get most of the economic benefit from narrow, domain-specific AI: curing diseases, scientific tools, automation, without creating a general agent that replaces us. That's where I'd put the effort. Not "how do we build superintelligence safely," but "do we need to build it at all?"

Am I hopeful that message wins? Not very. But I'd rather say it clearly and be wrong than stay quiet and be right.

r001.rationale: It mentions geopolitical competition and the difficulty of stopping a race, but does not say developers could continue in other jurisdictions during a geographically restricted pause.

r002.rationale: It says compute may get cheaper and advanced capabilities may need far less hardware, but does not argue that regulation would become ineffective if desktop computers could develop advanced AI.

r003.rationale: It does not identify regulatory compliance as a way to divert AI developers’ spending from compute to lawyers.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the intention behind them is good, and I signed the pause letter myself, so I'm not going to criticize people for trying. But we have to be honest about what actually happened. Six months passed, nobody paused, and the labs that signed or expressed sympathy kept training bigger models. So as a practical matter, the pause was a signal, not a mechanism.

The deeper problem is that regulation assumes you have a well-defined object to regulate. With nuclear weapons you can count warheads, you can inspect facilities, you know what enrichment looks like. With AI, the thing we're worried about is a capability that emerges from compute, data, and algorithms, and all three are getting cheaper and more distributed every year. You can put limits on compute today, and I think compute governance is probably the most promising lever we have, but it's a lever with an expiration date. Algorithmic efficiency improves, and what required a frontier cluster in 2024 runs on something much smaller a few years later.

And then there's the verification problem, which nobody has solved. If the United States and China agree to stop at some capability level, how do you check? You can't audit the weights of a model and read off how dangerous it is. We don't have a science of measuring these systems. We barely have a science of understanding what they do after we build them. So any treaty is really an agreement based on trust, and the incentives to cheat are enormous because the first mover gets everything.

So where does that leave me? I'd say I'm pessimistic about regulation as a solution, but I still support it as a way of buying time. Even a few years matters if you believe, as I do, that we don't currently know how to control a system smarter than us, and I don't see evidence we'll figure it out on the timelines the industry is working with. The honest position is that the only safe version of this is not building it, and I don't think any regulatory framework we've seen comes close to that. They're all designed around the assumption that we'll build it, and just build it responsibly. My concern is that "responsibly" is doing a lot of work in that sentence that nobody can actually cash out.

r002.rationale: It says compute limits may lose effectiveness as algorithms improve and hardware needs shrink, but does not argue that regulation would fail once advanced AI can be developed on a desktop.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention regulatory compliance diverting developers’ spending from compute to lawyers.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to distinguish between slowing down development and solving the safety problem. A pause could give us more time, but time is only useful if we know what to do with it. If we pause for six months and then resume the same race, we haven’t necessarily made anything safer.

Regulation can help, but it has to address the actual risk. Testing a system and finding no dangerous behavior is not the same as establishing that it will remain safe when it becomes more capable or operates in a new environment. And international coordination is difficult: you have competing companies, competing governments, and incentives to cut corners.

So I support efforts to slow down the development of systems we cannot reliably control. But I would want the condition for moving forward to be evidence of safety, rather than simply the passage of a particular amount of time. If we cannot provide that evidence, we should be willing to say that we are not ready.

r001.rationale: The response notes competing governments and difficulty coordinating internationally, but does not say developers could continue advanced AI development in jurisdictions outside a geographically restricted pause.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss desktop availability of compute or argue that this would make regulation ineffective.

r003.rationale: It does not identify compliance costs or lawyers as a way to redirect developers’ spending from compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a pause could buy us time, but only if it is enforceable and we know what we’re trying to accomplish during that time. A voluntary agreement among a few companies doesn’t solve the problem if other companies or governments continue pushing ahead.

The deeper issue is control. Before we build systems that are more capable than we are, we need good reasons to believe we can predict their behavior, constrain them, and shut them down. Being able to demonstrate impressive capabilities is not evidence that we can do those things.

So I support efforts to slow development and impose meaningful oversight. But regulation shouldn’t become a checklist that gives everyone permission to proceed. If we don’t know how to make a system safe, the responsible decision may be not to build it.
